author: Alana Loftus
title: Small plane forced to make emergency landing on busy highway - NewsBreak
text:
By Alana Loftus ,
1 hours ago A video has shown a small plane making an emergency landing on a crowded California highway during rush hour - miraculously avoiding hitting any cars.
The plane was a single engine Cessna T206 and sent an emergency message by radio to air traffic control moments before the emergency landing. According to logs on Live ATC.net reviewed by the KGTV, the pilot can be heard frantically saying, “Mayday! Mayday! 57-Lima Bravo (LB). Lost engine on left base.”
The plane touched down in the center median of the I-15 in San Diego around 4:45 pm on Monday. A shocking video shows the plane rolling down the middle of the highway.

Air Traffic Control reportedly tried to clear traffic on a runway for the pilot to land safely at a local airport, but the pilot said he did not think he’d make it that far.
“I can’t,” the pilot responded. “I can’t restart it. I think I might hit the 15.”
Stunned drivers looked on in horror as the plane landed in the patch of green between the lanes of traffic, miraculously avoiding all of the cars.
There were two people on board the plane at the time of the emergency landing, including the pilot. Both were uninjured in the incident, the Federal Aviation Administration said.
The official cause for the urgent landing has not been released by officials, but the pilot appeared to blame engine failure, according to KGTV. The incident remains under investigation.
The plane’s flight path on FlightAware shows that it took off from the nearby Montgomery-Gibbs Executive Airport at 3:50 p.m. It then flew along the coast to Oceanside.
The plane made a U-turn before it made the emergency landing. Rich Martindell, a retired aircraft accident investigator, told KGTV, “At the altitude he was at, when the motor quit, he didn’t have a lot of places to go. He picked a good one.”
The unbelievable incident came just a few days after a British skydiver survived a 11,000 feet freefall after both of his parachutes failed to open.
25-year-old Mitchell Deakin flew from the United Kingdom to Nevada to take part in a skydiving stunt that went terribly wrong. Miraculously, he and the instructor who he carried out the jump alongside, were not killed in the incident, though both suffered serious injuries.
